Creating Your Own Art Curriculum

Do you use an art curriculum? Maybe it’s a plan given by your district or even a sequence of lessons you’ve assembled yourself.

Or do you wish you had a plan, but the weeks fly by and every Sunday night is a scramble to figure out the week ahead?

Though there isn’t one right way to plan out your art program, it is important to design an art curriculum that serves you rather than agonizing over how to serve a meticulously planned out curriculum that steals your creative spontaneity and leaves you feeling like a robot.

New art teachers want to know how to plan their year. Seasoned teachers want to change things up.

When I was beginning my career, I felt the exact same way. I had never taught art before so I was overwhelmed at the idea of planning art lessons for an entire school of students. There were a few art books and resources that I turned to, but I knew I needed a plan.

What kind of art curriculum should I have? Did I need to follow standards? Were there any standards? What about art elements and principles? Did I have to tie into the teacher’s curriculum’s?

So I asked my Principal, “What do you expect from me?”

He said, “Just do art.”

Hmmmm. Okay.

Borrowing inspiration from the elements of art and principles of design, I tried art lessons that I found interesting. I experimented with different materials, different papers, different brushes until I found what worked. I took a stab at papier-mâché and 3-D art and lesson inspired by artists and art history. I gauged the success of the lessons by the student’s reactions. They provided the direction of my next lesson.

I feel my job is to introduce children to the world of art, to learn what it means to be creative and to learn techniques along the way. I think that’s what we all want to do with the privilege of teaching art to young students.

But how do you design the path to get there?

That’s where a thoughtfully designed elementary curriculum can make such a difference.

A curriculum gives you a path to follow so you’re not starting from scratch every week. It helps you see how skills and concepts build from one lesson to the next and from one grade level to another. And perhaps most importantly, it gives you the confidence that the projects you’re choosing aren’t just filling time, they’re helping students grow as artists.

The Perfect Art Curriculum

Here’s the thing: there is no one perfect curriculum.

Some might argue that there should be, but if there were, we wouldn’t have the freedom to experiment. Like the freedom to read a beautiful picture book and be inspired enough to create a lesson around it. Or to visit a museum and see a work of art that you just can’t wait to share with your classes. That’s what drives my love for teaching art. To introduce my students to new ways of seeing our world through the lens of art.

We encourage our members to use the 80/20 rule. When you plan for and structure 80% of your art program, you leave 20% for magic to happen.

Because a good curriculum shouldn’t box you in. It should give you enough structure that you have the freedom to be spontaneous.

That remaining 20% can leave room for the picture book you fall in love with, the artists you can’t wait to introduce or a seasonal project that you know your students will love.

So how do you plan for the 80%?

How do you create an elementary art curriculum?

Let’s dive in using these 4 steps for designing your own art curriculum.

Step 1: Choose an Overarching Theme

Choosing a theme just means deciding on a common thread between lessons. If you’re looking to streamline your planning, a theme is a great filter to pass those lesson ideas through to see if they fit.

Following a curriculum theme gives you the structure to see the big picture of your art program’s why or what you’re teaching, which is a great way to provide a framework for learning for your students.

Here are some of the most common themes, but the key isn’t finding the ‘perfect’ theme for your art curriculum. It’s choosing the one that excites you.

These are some of the curriculum frameworks we use inside The Sparklers’ Club, where teachers can choose from four complete K-7 curriculum’s depending on the kind of path they want for their students.

You might choose a:

Technique-Based Curriculum

Master one medium each month. This curriculum is all about developing craftsmanship and artistic techniques through experimentation with materials. This is actually the way that I began teaching my students. I relied on techniques that I knew and began teaching my students how to use watercolors, pastels and paint within a variety of subject matter. As my confidence and knowledge grew as a teacher, I added more materials and techniques.

If you are a new teacher or new to a school and unsure of student abilities or if you are a returning teacher but feel like your students are lacking in foundational art-making skills, this type of curriculum theme is really approachable.

Art History Curriculum

Art history-based curriculum’s focus on artists and art movements and move through time in a linear fashion.

They are great for recognizing how important art is in our world, both what has come before us and what is happening right now and for helping students make connections between art and the world around them. If introducing students to artists, movements and the stories behind artwork is central to your teaching, this can give your year a natural path to follow.

Global Art Curriculum

Have you ever felt like you want to go deeper with your art program and explore the world that we live in?

Learning about communities and cultures through art can help connect students to the beautiful things in our world. It can facilitate deeper connections to each other and our world that can lead to understanding, compassion and create a sense of community in your school.

If one of your goals is helping students see that art is everywhere and that people around the world use art to express ideas, traditions and experiences, this can be a meaningful framework for your year.

Art Theory Curriculum

An art theory curriculum focuses on providing students with knowledge of the elements of art and the principles of design in a sequential, skill-building framework.

This is a great choice for new art teachers or teachers who would like to build a solid art education foundation for their students.

Step 2: Create Units Based on the Curriculum Theme

What curriculum theme do you identify with most?

The next step is to break that theme into manageable units based on the number of art sessions you will have with your students.

For example, if you choose an art history-based curriculum theme and you expect that you will be able to realistically complete nine multi-session art projects with each grade, you know that you need to divide your year into nine art history units.

Each of the units could cover a different period in art history or an artist that represents a movement. Depending on your theme, your units could be “Line” or “Impressionism” or “Watercolors” or “South America.” 

Ok, quick check-in. How are your plans coming along? Feeling like things are piecing together for your art program?

So now you have an overarching theme that you’ve broken into manageable units. Next, let’s talk about lesson objectives. I promise it’s not as scary as it sounds!

Step 3: Decide Your Lesson Objectives

Within each unit, you’ll need to find or develop lessons for each grade that fit the unit, but before you go on the hunt for lessons (and jump to Step 4!), identify what you are trying to teach. 

The fancy way of describing this objective building is called creating a “scope and sequence.”

A scope and sequence is simply a plan of why you are teaching certain concepts and deciding on the order in which you plan to teach them.

Making a scope and sequence, or a linear plan for your year is one of the easiest ways to build an elementary art curriculum map for learning that can help both you and your students know both where you’re going and where you’ve been. 

An easy way to look at this is with the elements of art and principles of design.

You can see how the objectives flow naturally from one to the other, from drawing lines, then using lines to make shapes, then using both lines and shapes to create patterns and finally beginning to look at the beginning stages of color theory by using primary colors. 

With a theme set, units decided and learning objectives in place, you are well on your way to knowing what kind of lessons you need to fill in your art curriculum, which brings us to…

Step 4: Add Lessons

Do you notice how the lessons come last in our steps? It seems counterintuitive because it’s often lessons that have the lead when we think about our art program!

But keeping them as the last step saves us from questioning and second-guessing because now we have our framework in place with an overarching theme that has been broken in units and then clear guidance in place with lesson objectives. 

Now we use those very specific intentions and goals to point to lessons that will fit our curriculum design. 

It’s the best part, in my opinion, when I’ve narrowed down the specifications so that there is a clear path to the art project that checks all the boxes. 

With my curriculum designed, I can teach with confidence, from a place of knowing the direction my art program is headed and the lessons I will teach to get there.

Now, here are my questions for you….

Do you have a curriculum set for you or do you get the freedom to create your own?

What are the biggest obstacles you face in creating your own art curriculum?

What’s the main goal you have for your art program?

      • Jenn
        August 26, 2011 at 4:53 pm

        Kinders are a challenge. Each year you forget because by the end of the year they are following along so great. I do a lot of “song and dance” so to say to draw them in. If I am having them try to follow along I often have to get them all paying attention, like you said they are talking out loud, or off task. I will often have everyone put their hands on their head when they are ready to go on. You can also have them repeat after you with a silly rhyme that goes along with what you are teaching. Talk to them and present things like they are magical, fun and exciting. The first few weeks are the trickiest with the little ones. You really need to enforce the rules while keeping their attention at the same time making it fun and engaging. I do a great lesson at the beginning of each year with line for my kinders and first graders. We sing the different types of line to the song of ” wheels on the bus” I have them repeat each line after me and we draw in the air or on the table with our finger as we sing the song. Then we put it all together and run through it . Next we draw them on paper. Here is the song if you are interested. A curved line arcs all around, A wavy line bumps up and down, A zigzag line has points you see, won’t you sing along with me. A spiral line goes round and round, a broken line will skip the ground, some are thick and some are thin, lines can do so many things. A vertical line goes up and down, A horizontal line lies on the ground, diagonal lines slant side to side and that’s what I know about lines. Good luck and have fun with it. You can change up the accents for the first graders they like to sing it western style, British accent, robot, what ever you can think of. There is also a cute lesson on the internet about a monster that comes to school that teaches the rules. I took the story and changed the words to fit into the art room that gave specific good and bad choices to teach my art room rules. Then we talk about not being an art monster when we come to art. Also there is a simple follow along monster drawing you can do with crayons and one paint color (crayon resist). I just started with this lesson myself this past week. Then when the students break a rule I reference the story about making good choices and not to act like the art monster. I borrowed this idea from an awesome teacher I saw on Artsonia from Ceeder Creek Elementary, Linda Welling (Not sure on the spelling ) and adapted it for my needs. Between Patty’s Deep Space Sparkle and searching through Artsonia I have found so many wonderful lessons and ideas. Love to share and find new inspiration on here from all the comments and blogs.
